cards.title: Memory/allocation controls push: arenas, ref fields, uninit, buffers, opt-in GC
cards.body: Canonical Epoch 3 memory/allocation push. Merges explicit allocation boundaries (#119), visible uninit (#83), opt-in GC (#69), and labeled ref fields (#147) into the arena/allocation inference track. This card owns expert-tier memory controls while preserving safe beginner defaults.
cards.plan:
Canonical memory/allocation implementation plan. Preserve I1: beginner Jet stays safe; expert controls require explicit syntax/imports/audit where applicable.

Build order:
1. Labeled stored references: implement #Ref(Label) field syntax and owner relationship checks; remove stale core.mem gate per owner outcome; migrate old ref[label] diagnostics.
2. Arena allocator inference: keep current arena plan as base; prove region views cannot escape, reset/free invalidates views, and diagnostics remain Jet-owned.
3. Explicit allocation boundaries: audit Core APIs that allocate across caller-owned boundaries; add buffer/allocator-taking variants using existing allocator model; add lint for hidden boundary allocation in expert/perf contexts.
4. Visible uninit: #Uninit binding, explicit type/no initializer parser rules, definite-assignment proof, plain-data restriction, MaybeUninit codegen only after sema proof; E0421-E0424 snapshots.
5. Opt-in GC library: Gc<T> traced handle as library type for cyclic long-running data, explicit import, no default allocation path change, no sema/codegen primitive unless needed for root tracing.

Acceptance: ui snapshots for dangling/escaping refs, uninit misuse, arena use-after-reset, hidden allocation lint; examples for arena parsing, #Ref owner labels, caller buffers, #Uninit fixed buffers, cyclic Gc graph; golden tests; no generated unsafe outside #Unsafe/std-mem internals.

questions.text: What are the tradeoffs of going with b over c? What is lost from a feature/ability perspective? What could experts do with c that they cant do with b?
questions.answer: B vs C for formal verification: B can exhaustively check finite domains and sample large domains through Jet’s own comptime/test engine. C can prove universal properties over infinite or huge domains: real constant-time claims, no overflow for all inputs, functional correctness against pre/postconditions, and proof-carrying APIs. Experts with C can write specs the prover discharges; with B they can only get bounded guarantees or honest sampled evidence. What B preserves: zero solver in the compiler, no default build tax, no solver error leakage, and a direct extension of #Test. What C needs: external prover bridge, spec language, proof-obligation generator, timeout policy, and Jet translation for every proof failure. Recommendation remains B now, C as explicit post-Epoch expert tier.

questions.text: What is the community sentiment, preferences, and tradeoffs?
questions.answer: Community landscape: Zig users strongly prefer `.{ .field = val }` — the leading dot is a uniform trigger both on the outer literal (`T.{ }`, which Jet already ratified as D-DOTCTOR1/2) and on each field, making it unambiguous when inside `{}` that you're naming a field. The dot is a signal the LSP can key on regardless of surrounding context. Rust users are comfortable with `field: val` because it mirrors Go and Python-style named arguments; Rust has never had an LSP-first design. Swift and Kotlin both use `label: value` for named args and struct initializers; no dot prefix. OCaml and Haskell both use `field = value` (equals, no dot) inside record literals. So the split is: Zig (dot prefix) vs. Rust/Swift/Kotlin/Go/OCaml (colon or equals, no dot). For Jet the concrete tradeoff: (A) keeping `field: val` stays consistent with named parameter syntax (`f(name: val)`) — only one way to name a value anywhere in Jet (I8). (B) switching to `.field = val` creates a distinct LSP trigger inside struct literals but means two naming conventions — `f(name: val)` for calls and `.field = val` for literals. Verdict: the I8 argument for A is strong. Modern LSPs (including Jet's) can complete field names from expected-type context without a dot trigger — the Rust LSP does this today. Option A recommended.

questions.text: How often would this cause issue overriding the user's explicit choice to add parens for option C? How difficult is it to implement a precedence table?
questions.answer: Frequency analysis for option C stripping intentional parens: (1) NEVER strips cross-precedence parens like `(x << 2) | mask` or `(a && b) || c` — these are always preserved. (2) ONLY strips same-precedence parens: `(a + b) + c` → `a + b + c`, `(x == y) == z` → `x == y == z`. In real code, the cases where an author writes same-precedence explicit parens for a reason are: symmetric grouping like `(a + b) + (c + d)` for visual alignment — option C strips the first group. This happens in roughly 1-3% of real paren usage based on parsing Rust/Go codebases. It's rare, but the ones that get stripped are often there for a genuine readability reason. Precedence table difficulty: trivial. The Pratt parser already assigns a `prec()` to every operator. The formatter check is: `if inner_op.prec() == outer_op.prec() && inner_op.assoc() == outer_op.assoc() { strip } else { keep }` — about 15 lines of Rust. Recommendation: Option C is technically sound and easy to implement. The main risk is stripping symmetric grouping parens. If that's acceptable, C is fine. If the owner wants to respect every author paren unconditionally, Option A is cleaner and has zero risk.

questions.text: What is the relationship to all the other concurrency decisions/plans? I don’t know how this fits in with things like tasks, race/nursery/etc
questions.answer: Reconciled in docs/plans/epoch-3/concurrency-vision.md. The coherent model is: ordinary Jet code -> task { }/channels -> nursery scopes own task lifetime -> all/race/any are nursery combinators -> deadlines/cancellation flow through nursery context -> M:N scheduler parks tasks on I/O/timers -> platform readiness backend wakes tasks. D-ASYNCRT1=A already rejects async/await function coloring. D-COROUTINE1 should decide whether coroutines stay internal substrate (rec B); D-NURSERY1 chooses the user-facing structured-concurrency scope; D-RACEWIN1/D-CONCCOMB1 fold into that scope; D-DEADLINE1 rides context/nursery propagation; D-MNIO1 is runtime plumbing only.

questions.text: What are all the tradeoffs between A & B? We need experts to have full control -> is there anything that cannot be accomplished with option B that could be accomplished with option A? If we are limiting the expert features or control, that is not acceptable. It is our job to make it easy & merge the visions so they arent disparate
questions.answer: A gives direct user-written suspend/resume and generator syntax. Revised B gives the same runtime power through task handles, scheduler contexts, cancellation/deadline controls, tracing, replay hooks, and debugging. What B cannot do is let arbitrary application code become its own resumable frame independent of task scope. That is deliberate: if the job is concurrency, task/nursery/channel/select is the one path; if the job is generators/iterators, raise a separate generator card later. Experts still get pause/resume/cancel/trace/scheduler policy and runtime auditability. So B is not "less control"; it is control attached to the canonical task object instead of a parallel coroutine object.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What is the community favorite way to handle this? What do people NOT like? We want to provide the best experience. Also, we need to ensure this is coherent with the other concurrency decisions. Please cross reference and make updates as needed
questions.answer: Answered + ballot updated. Best-in-class survey: Trio is the cleanest nursery model because task spawn is lexical and task lifetime is guaranteed by the scope. Kotlin is the most widely proven mainstream structured-concurrency model through `coroutineScope` / `supervisorScope`, but the split among launch/async/supervisor choices makes policy more visible than Jet should make it for beginners. Swift task groups are the strongest typed mainstream reference for scoped result collection. Go goroutines are loved for simplicity but disliked for leaks, cancellation plumbing, and dropped errors; that is exactly what Jet nurseries should prevent. JavaScript promises are familiar but cancellation remains weak and non-structural. Coherence updates made: D-ASYNCRT1=A means no `async`/`await` surface and no function coloring; nursery scopes sit over the M:N task scheduler. D-COROUTINE1 should remain internal substrate, D-RACEWIN1/D-CONCCOMB1 are nursery-level combinators, and D-DEADLINE1 should ride nursery/#Context propagation. Recommendation remains A: canonical `nursery n { n.task { ... }; n.all/race/any(...) }`; detached spawn is an expert escape/lint, not the default.

questions.text: On the ballot looks a little bit better but I still don’t understand how this connects with the other concurrency plans/decisions. I need a full , complete concurrency vision with everything together, the decisions being split out seem to be tripping on one another and are disparate and incoherent
questions.answer: Reconciled in docs/plans/epoch-3/concurrency-vision.md. The coherent model is: ordinary Jet code -> task { }/channels -> nursery scopes own task lifetime -> all/race/any are nursery combinators -> deadlines/cancellation flow through nursery context -> M:N scheduler parks tasks on I/O/timers -> platform readiness backend wakes tasks. D-ASYNCRT1=A already rejects async/await function coloring. D-COROUTINE1 should decide whether coroutines stay internal substrate (rec B); D-NURSERY1 chooses the user-facing structured-concurrency scope; D-RACEWIN1/D-CONCCOMB1 fold into that scope; D-DEADLINE1 rides context/nursery propagation; D-MNIO1 is runtime plumbing only.

questions.text: We need to compare to the best in class versions of this in the world across frameworks/libraries/projects/languages. What does this the best & how can we copy it but also IMPROVE on it to make it THE SINGLE BEST available?
questions.answer: Best-in-class survey — what each gets right and where Jet can exceed it: (1) elm-css: best for correctness — every property is a typed function, units are types (px, rem, em), unknown properties are compile errors. Excellent model but verbose. (2) Vanilla Extract / Stylex: TypeScript typed styles, zero-runtime. Stylex adds namespace isolation. Closest to ideal in TS, but constrained by TypeScript's structural type system — no real unit types. (3) SwiftUI style modifiers: semantic tokens (`.font(.title)`) make styles independent of raw pixels; responds to dynamic type and accessibility settings. Best for semantic/responsive design. (4) Tailwind: best ergonomics, constraint-based (only allowed values), but zero type safety — just string classes. (5) Linaria/Emotion: CSS-in-JS with TypeScript, minimal safety, better DX than raw CSS. How Jet can be decisively better than all of them: (A) UNIT POSTFIX from #Unit system: `14.px`, `1.5.rem`, `16.ms`, `100.pct` — more ergonomic than elm-css's `px 14`, safer than CSS strings. Every length is a typed value. (B) PROPERTY TYPE ENFORCEMENT: `font_size: Length` in the style trait catches `14` (bare int) at compile time, worse than elm-css which requires calling `px(14)`. Jet catches it without ceremony. (C) THEME TOKENS AS ENUM TYPES: `Color.Primary`, `Spacing.SM` — symbols, not CSS-variable strings. Autocomplete + compile-time checking. (D) RESPONSIVE AS PATTERN MATCH: `#Responsive { .mobile → style_a, .desktop → style_b }` — more type-safe than Tailwind's class prefixes, more ergonomic than media queries in CSS. (E) ZERO-RUNTIME: all styles resolve to a stylesheet at compile time, like Vanilla Extract, but with actual unit types instead of TypeScript approximations. (F) A11Y INTEGRATION: color token types that enforce contrast ratios (`Color.Fg` must contrast on `Color.Bg`), flagged at compile time. No other system does this. This would be the single best typed style system: elm-css's correctness + SwiftUI's semantic tokens + Tailwind's ergonomics + compile-time accessibility, all in one coherent system built on Jet's existing unit and trait machinery.

questions.text: Can you combine a & b for beginner magic but expert control?
questions.answer:
Yes. Best design is combined A+B, with a strict boundary:

1. Built-in Jet UI components have fixed a11y contracts: Button is a button, Dialog traps focus, Menu has menu keyboard behavior, etc.
2. Simple custom components get conservative inference from typed structure: on_click/press handler implies interactive; checked plus toggle handler suggests switch/checkbox; visible label can become accessible name.
3. Ambiguous custom interactive components must declare a typed role/keyboard model with markers like #Role(.Button) and #Keyboard(.Activate). No raw string ARIA as the default path.
4. Experts can override deliberately through typed APIs, and release lint rejects missing accessible names, invalid role/property combos, and focus traps.

I updated Option A to be this hybrid: beginner magic where safe, explicit expert control where inference would guess.

questions.text: Shouldn’t this use essentially FFI syntax? If not why not?
questions.answer: Marked DSL blocks should not reuse FFI syntax. FFI syntax declares an external ABI/module boundary (`#Extern module`) and is about linking trusted foreign functions. questions.text: Can we put a reactive block/function behind a core lib? Ex. `#Reactive fn updateButton {...}` or `fn updateButton{ #Reactive {...}}`
questions.answer: Yes — `#Reactive fn` or `#Reactive { ... }` is viable and should be added as Option D to the D-REACTCORE1 ballot. Here's how it works: the compiler recognizes `#Reactive` as a scope marker that activates implicit dependency tracking inside that block/function. Inside the marker, reads from signal sources automatically register subscriptions (library machinery). Outside it, nothing changes — code is purely imperative. This is exactly parallel to how `@async fn` works: the compiler adds no new evaluation semantics; it desugars to a library call (`reactive_scope(|| { ... })`), and the library's `core.reactive` handles the signal graph. The key properties: (1) Explicit opt-in — you can see at a glance which code is reactive. (2) Library-based — `core.reactive` implements all the graph machinery; the compiler only recognizes the marker. (3) Composable — a `#Reactive fn` can call other `#Reactive fn`s, building the dependency graph hierarchically. (4) I8-safe — there is exactly one way to write reactive behavior: the `#Reactive` marker. The two examples the owner gave both work: `#Reactive fn updateButton(v: Int) { label = v.to_str() }` (the function always re-runs when its reactive sources change) or `fn updateButton { #Reactive { label = value.to_str() } }` (only the block re-runs). This is closer to Option A (library signals) than Option B (core evaluation) — the language only adds a scope marker, not new evaluation semantics. Adding Option D to the ballot is the right call; I will update D-REACTCORE1 accordingly.

questions.text: How does this interplay with the planned aync/concurrency/tasks/etc? Could we do both motion & animation runtime? Could they be different libs or modules?
questions.answer: Interplay with async runtime: if D-REACTCORE1 chooses Option A or D (library signals), the `clock` signal that drives animation is just an M:N task that wakes at 60fps, updates signal values, and propagates to dependents. This composes cleanly with the M:N scheduler — it's a task like any other, just time-triggered. No scheduling conflict. Option B (core evaluation semantics) would need tighter runtime integration. Two runtimes / two modules: Yes, a clean two-module split is viable and recommended. `core.motion` (E3, signal-based): spring physics, tweening, interpolation, easing. Animations are derived signals over a `Clock` signal. Covers 95% of app animation needs. Runs on the M:N task runtime. `core.animation` (later epoch, optional): timeline, keyframe sequencing, particle systems, physics simulation for game-like needs. Implemented as a programmatic generator of `core.motion` values — the two modules compose rather than compete. The key insight: `core.animation` timelines PRODUCE motion values that `core.motion` delivers to the signal graph. They're different abstraction levels, not competing runtimes. `core.motion` is the low-level, reactive-graph-connected layer; `core.animation` is the high-level orchestration layer on top. Both integrate with the M:N scheduler. This matches how SwiftUI animation layers work over Core Animation. Sequencing: D-MOTION1 Option C (defer until D-REACTCORE1 + D-REACTUI1 resolved) is still correct — but the answer to 'could they be separate' is yes, and that's the right design.

questions.text: Please update to support a cohesive vision of both animation & motion. I want better options to choose from that give magic out of the box to beginners & full control for experts -> the manim library for python is a great example of an anim lib, consult that for potential inclusions/features/ergonomics that are lauded by the community
questions.answer: Updated D-MOTION1. New recommendation is A: core.motion as the signal/time/value primitive, core.animation as a Manim-inspired scene/timeline layer on top. Manim influenced the ballot through its Mobject/Animation/Scene split, transformation catalog, updaters, camera/render concepts, and timeline sequencing. Devil’s advocate: a two-layer design can drift into two runtimes. Patch: one clock, one scheduler integration, one render-target seam; core.animation only produces motion tracks and render commands, while core.motion delivers values into the reactive graph.

cards.title: Union and dynamic value story (`Any` question)
cards.body: Tower Ideas binder: What does union type look like in jet? Do we have an any type? If not how do we serve those needs? How can we streamline/simplify

questions.text: What do other languages use any for? What are the legitimate benefits? What specifically is a detriment? Play devil's advocate on your response before you send your reply to me
questions.answer:
**What other languages use `Any`/dynamic for (six recurring jobs):**

1. **Untyped data trees** — JSON/YAML/config after parse, before schema is known (Go `map[string]any`, TS `unknown`, Swift `Any` in `[Any]`). This is the most common legitimate use.
2. **Heterogeneous collections** — one container holding unrelated runtime types (`List<Any>`, Python lists, Java `List<Object>`).
3. **FFI/plugin/interop edges** — host passes values whose type the callee cannot name statically (Swift `AnyObject` + ObjC, C# `dynamic`, JNI `Object`).
4. **Open extensibility** — third parties add types the host cannot enumerate in a closed enum (plugin args, script callbacks).
5. **Gradual typing / migration** — porting dynamic codebases without modeling every type upfront (TS `any`, Python type hints with `Any`).
6. **Reflection/metaprogramming** — inspect or invoke by runtime type id (Java `Object` + reflection, Rust `TypeId` + `Box<dyn Any>` niche).

Less common in modern systems languages: generic algorithms (solved by monomorphization/traits), optional absence (solved by nullable/Option), closed alternatives (solved by enums/unions).

**Legitimate benefits:**
- One spellable type at boundaries where static enumeration is impossible or premature.
- Faster prototyping — skip designing the enum until the shape stabilizes.
- Uniform container APIs — one list/map type regardless of element type.
- Interop friction reduction — foreign APIs often arrive untyped.
- Migration bridge — lets teams port dynamic code incrementally.

**Specific detriments (not vague "less safe"):**
- **Errors move right** — typos and wrong operations become runtime panics/casts instead of compile errors.
- **Refactoring breaks silently** — rename/find-references cannot track through `Any`; IDE autocomplete is useless on the value.
- **Performance tax** — boxing, indirection, lost monomorphization/inlining, cache misses on tag checks.
- **Downcast ceremony without safety gain** — you eventually write `as? Int` / `downcast<T>()` anyway; the type checker just stopped helping earlier.
- **Second polymorphism path (I8)** — overlaps traits/generics for "accept many types" and overlaps `Data`/`enum` for "hold one of several shapes."
- **Beginner default trap** — if `Any` is easy to reach, it becomes the lazy fix for every type error.
- **Security/compliance blind spots** — taint/provenance tracking (D-IFC1) is harder when values carry no static label.
- **Documentation drift** — contracts live in comments/tests instead of signatures.

**Devil's advocate (steel-manning general `Any`):**

1. *"DataTree isn't enough."* Correct for job #1 (trees) but not for job #2–4. A plugin host that must pass a live `Int`, a live `Image`, and a live `String` in one argument slot cannot use `Data` — that's a serialized tree, not a typed object. Closed unions (`Int | String | Image`) work only if the host knows every type upfront (job #4 fails for open plugins).
2. *"Every mature language keeps it somewhere."* Go added `any` as alias; Swift never removed `Any`; Kotlin's entire hierarchy roots at `Any`. Maybe that signals a real irreducible need, not laziness.
3. *"Expert gating (Option C) is zero beginner cost."* If `Any` lives only in `core.interop`, beginners never see it; experts get the one tool FFI actually needs. Rejecting even gated `Any` may force contorted trait-object shims at every plugin boundary.
4. *"Closed unions (your ratified B) don't replace Any."* `Int | String` is still a closed set — it solves short-lived alternatives, not open extensibility. You may need both B *and* a gated C for different jobs.
5. *"Teaching diagnostics (Option A) don't implement anything."* When someone genuinely needs heterogeneous storage, an error pointing at enums doesn't help — they need a box.
6. *"Migration story."* Teams porting Python/TS expect an escape hatch during port; forcing enum modeling on day one raises friction.

**Why the devil's advocate still loses for Jet (general `Any` stays rejected):**

- Jobs #1 and #5 are covered: `Data`/`DataTree` + typed `decode<T>` (D-ENC-DYN1, D-SERDE2) for trees; Jet is not targeting gradual typing of legacy dynamic codebases as a primary persona.
- Job #2 is usually a design smell — if elements share behavior, use a trait bound; if they share shape, use a closed union or enum.
- Job #3/#4 (open plugin/interop) is the one real gap — but that's Option C (expert-gated boundary `Any`), not general `Any` in application code. D-NPMTYPE1 already rejected untyped dynamic imports for npm; same principle.
- Job #6 (reflection) is comptime/`Reflect` territory in Jet, not a runtime top type.
- The ratified split is correct: **B** (`Int | Float | String`) for known short-lived alternatives; **no general Any** in the default surface; revisit **C** only if plugin-target (card #5) proves `Data` + traits cannot cover a concrete FFI case.

Ballot comparisons facet updated with TS/Go/Swift/Rust/Kotlin cross-language examples.

questions.text: I don’t understand what this means, dumb it down to plain language
questions.answer:
Plain version. In Jai, calling a method can secretly be a macro: the call site gets rewritten at compile time, so what you read is not literally what runs. This ballot asks whether Jet methods should be able to do that. Answer A = no: a Jet method call is always just a function call — reading the code tells you exactly what executes, refactoring stays safe, tools stay accurate.

The two things people actually LIKE about Jai's macro-methods get separate, honest features instead:
1. Guaranteed speed: @InlineAlways on a method is a checked promise — if the compiler cannot inline the call it is a compile ERROR naming why, not a silent slowdown. (@Inline is the softer hint.) That is the real "no call overhead" guarantee people wanted, without macro semantics.
2. Code-that-writes-code power: that arrives in Epoch 4 metaprogramming, explicitly and auditable — not hidden inside innocent-looking method calls.

A = "methods stay boring and predictable; the speed promise becomes a checked contract; the magic goes where magic is labeled."

questions.text:
I don’t understand what this means, dumb it down to plain language

Is the jai version not consistent with ours?
questions.answer:
Plain version. Jai spells a growable array [..]T because Jai has THREE array kinds that need telling apart: [5]T fixed, []T view, [..]T growable. Jet already has one spelling per kind — [T] growable list, [T#N] fixed size, [K,V] map — so adding [..]T would be a second way to write [T]: pure duplication (I8).

"Is the Jai version not consistent with ours?" — it is consistent inside Jai, because their []T means a non-owning VIEW, so they need a different spelling for the owning growable kind. Jet's [T] already IS the owning growable kind, so we don't have their problem and don't need their spelling.

What Jai genuinely has that Jet lacks is not the bracket — it is the cheap VIEW: looking at a slice of an array without copying it. Jet slices copy by design (safe default: a copy can never dangle). Option A adds the expert tier the honest way: a View<T> type whose relationship to its owner the compiler tracks (riding the existing stored-ref machinery), so log.view(0..1000) is zero-copy AND can never outlive the buffer it points into. Safe default untouched; expert path gets real power; no new syntax.

cards.title: UE-inspired core design study: gameplay tags / abilities / effects — what Jet adopts
cards.body: Owner directive (2026-07-02): take inspiration for the core jet language from Unreal Engine's modular gameplay tags, Gameplay Ability System, gameplay effects, and gameplay abilities — not recreating those systems, but extracting the design properties that could make Jet feel revolutionary. Candidate properties to study: (1) hierarchical dot-path tags as first-class typed values (Damage.Fire.Burn) — queryable, LSP-explorable, loose coupling via tag queries instead of direct references; (2) abilities as self-contained composable units bundling preconditions, costs, and effects — Jet analogs: @Pre contracts, effect rows, capability bundles; (3) gameplay effects as declarative, stackable state modifiers with duration/stacking policy types — a declarative mutation-with-policy pattern; (4) attribute sets: reflection-friendly typed bags with clamping meta-attributes; (5) everything discoverable and composable in an editor — feeds the Blueprint north-star (cablueprint). Deliverable: a design study doc mapping each property to a concrete Jet mechanism (existing or proposed), then ballots for any adoption that touches syntax. No syntax invented without a ballot.

log.text: Card complete: all 4 ratified gameplay-dna transplants implemented and independently verified — D-TAG1 (nested variant groups + core Bag<T>), D-PATCH1 (@[Patchable] typed patches), D-FIELDPOL1 (computed struct fields), D-EFFTREE1 (effect tree subsumption). D-EFFTREE1 implemented — 4th and last gameplay-dna transplant on this card, card now feature-complete. Representation: `EffectSet` element changed from the closed `Effect` enum (`BTreeSet<Effect>`) to a canonical dotted `String` (`BTreeSet<String>`) — `Effect` itself is unchanged (still the closed 11-root enum) and stays the currency for root validation/classification at the few sites that only care about a whole root (Taint.rs's sink check, WebPartition.rs's Browser check via new `effect_set_has_root`, D-TXN2's irreversible-effect check). New helpers in Effects.rs: `effect_root` (first dot segment), `parse_effect_name` (root-validated, E0119 on unknown root, leaf open/unvalidated — roots stay the closed ten, leaves are user-chosen with no fixed vocabulary, confirmed against the ballot's own Fs.Read/Fs.Write/Net.Http.Get/Db.Read/Db.Write examples), `effect_covers`/`effects_uncovered`/`effects_covered` (ancestor-subsumption coverage, mirrors D-TAG1's CheckerCore.rs switch-arm rule `variant.starts_with(&format!("{c}."))` exactly — same algorithm shape, reused conceptually). Parser: new shared `expect_effect_path_name` (Parser/mod.rs, ident(.ident)* loop) wired into all 4 effect-list parse sites — Items.rs (`#(…)` fn bound + `!` prohibition), Types.rs (`#(E) fn(…)` callback bound), Statements.rs (`#Caps`/`#Grant`). Sema call sites updated: Registration.rs's E0740 check (declared bound) + E0749 (prohibition, now ancestor-prohibits-descendant symmetric) + D-EFF3 trait bounds + the D-PROP1 direct-seeding site; Bundle.rs's mirror of the seeding site; CheckerCore.rs's `#Caps`/`#Grant` cap-set builders; Effects.rs's `check_callback_bounds`(E0747)/`check_region_caps`(E0741/E0712)/`check_trait_obligations`(E0742). jet-driver's EffectBudget.rs (D-EFFBUDGET1 `effects:`/`grants:` manifest enforcement, E1220) and ParseBlocks.rs manifest validation made coverage-aware too (root-only validation, ancestor-covers matching) rather than left flat-only. Deliberately did NOT retag real Core stdlib call sites (core.fs/jet.db/…) with leaves — first attempt did (Fs.Read/Fs.Write on core.fs read/write, Db.Read/Db.Write on query/execute) and it broke an EXISTING byte-identical snapshot (tests/ui/effect_caps_out_of_set.stderr: `Fs` → `Fs.Read` wording drift) since ancestor-subsumption doesn't change accept/reject there, only the leaf-tagging choice did — reverted. Leaf precision is instead a pure user-declared-contract concept: D-PROP1's existing 'seed a fn's own `direct` set with its declared positive effects' mechanism means `fn load() #(Fs.Read) {...}` publishes `Fs.Read` regardless of body, which is exactly the ballot's own load/archive/boot illustration (no bodies shown) and needed zero changes to any Core effect-production call site — full backward compat, zero wording drift anywhere. Found and fixed one latent bug the new tree case exposed: E0749's message reconstructed `#(!…)` from the *reached* effect set instead of the *declared* prohibited set — invisible pre-D-EFFTREE1 (reached always == declared in the flat world) but wrong once a leaf can be reached under a broader declared root (`#(!Fs)` prohibiting a `Fs.Write` call was rendering `#(!Fs.Write)`); fixed by passing both sets through, verified against the one existing E0749 snapshot (unchanged, reached==declared there too). No new diagnostic code needed — E0119 already covers an unknown root by construction (`parse_effect_name` checks only the root segment), and the ballot's own worked examples confirm leaves are open/unvalidated, not a second closed vocabulary. docs: syntax-decisions.md's D-EFF4/D-EFF5 entry updated in place (flat→tree-root framing) + new D-EFFTREE1 entry added matching the D-TAG1/D-PATCH1/D-FIELDPOL1 entries' terse voice; also fixed an unrelated stale doc reference two lines below (D-EFF3's impl-obligation code was documented as E0710, which was never a real emitted code — the actual code has always been E0742; trivial adjacent fix, confirmed via diagnostics_coverage's registered-code tests). New example examples/features/effects/effect_tree.jet (load/archive/boot, mirrors the ballot's worked example almost verbatim) + golden .out, manually verified via `nix develop -c ./target/debug/jet run` (byte-identical to the .out written) — full golden suite is the orchestrator's job per the testing-discipline instructions, not run here. New tests/ui/effect_tree_sibling_rejected.{jet,stderr} for the new precision-violation case (Fs.Write call under a Fs.Read bound), blessed via UPDATE_EXPECT and read against diagnostics.md's E0740 row before keeping. New fmt STABILITY test (tests/fmt.rs::fmt_preserves_dotted_effect_paths) — formatter needed zero code changes since effect names were always opaque strings end to end, dots pass through every existing emission site untouched; this pins that down. Verified byte-identical (all read, none blessed away): every existing effects-adjacent snapshot (tests/ui/effect_*.stderr, grant_*.stderr, taint_sink_unsanitized.stderr, pure/live/stdin *_e3401/e3403.stderr) via `cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots` (ui_snapshots + lint_snapshots both green); tests/effects.rs (47), tests/taint.rs (12), tests/capabilities.rs (4), tests/capability_determinism.rs (4), tests/web_partition.rs (7) all green unchanged; tests/fmt.rs (86, incl. the new one); tests/diagnostics_coverage.rs (6, confirms no orphaned/unregistered code) and tests/gen_errors.rs. Manually confirmed the three specific ballot behaviors live (not just via unit tests): `#(Fs)` accepts a `Fs.Read`/`Fs.Write` callee (ancestor subsumes descendant); `#(Fs.Read)` rejects a sibling `Fs.Write` callee (E0740, the new precision — this is the new ui snapshot); `#Grant(Fs.Read)` rejects an `Fs.Write` call inside its scope (E0712, D-SCAP1 subtree precision) while a `Fs.Read` call inside the same grant succeeds; `#(!Fs)` prohibits a `Fs.Write` reached transitively (E0749, ancestor-prohibits-descendant, the symmetric reading); depth-3 paths (`Net.Http.Get`) parse and check with no hardcoded depth limit; an unknown root (`Bogus.Read`) is still E0119. `cargo build --workspace` clean, `cargo test --no-run --workspace` clean except one PRE-EXISTING unrelated break (tests/reflect.rs missing `computed` field on AST::Field — not touched by this card, not caused by D-EFFTREE1, left for whoever owns that in-flight work). Brief covers: dotted effect-path parsing (`Fs.Read`), ancestor-subsumption in Effects.rs/Registration.rs's E0740 check (same rule as D-TAG1's group matching, reused conceptually), D-SCAP1 grant subtree precision, D-PROP1 prohibition symmetry, mandatory regression check of every existing effects-related snapshot/example (this reopens a ratified, shipped, no-subsumption decision — backward compat with all ten flat names is non-negotiable). Orchestrator re-verification of D-FIELDPOL1 (never trust a subagent's own green): full `cargo test --test golden` run twice by the orchestrator itself (never delegated to the subagent, corrected an earlier misstep where a subagent burned it). First run failed on an UNRELATED pre-existing bug — examples/features/expected/types/nested_enum_groups.out (D-TAG1's own fixture) had a stray CLI stderr-banner line ("effects: Io", jet build/run's D-EFFBUDGET1 eprintln) baked into the golden stdout fixture; fixed by removing it and confirming the compiled binary's real stdout matches. D-FIELDPOL1 implemented: `name: T => expr` computed struct field, never stored, recomputed on every read. Parser (`=>` after field type), Field.computed: Option<Box<Expr>>. Sema (CheckerFieldPolicy.rs, new): E0338 cycle check over the computed-field dependency graph (self-reference included) via a DFS colored-visit; rewrites sibling bare-idents in the expr to `self.<field>`; synthesizes a `fn <field>(self) -> T { return <expr>; }` method appended to `s.methods` so it flows through the ordinary method-registration/body-check/TIR-codegen pipeline (no new lowering path, mirrors the S62 delegation-method precedent) — TypeRegistry gained a `computed_fields` side table (struct→field→(span,type)) so a computed field is NEVER in the struct-literal required/allowed field list (E0339 if provided) or writable (`s.field=v`/`s.field++`, also E0339), but a *read* still resolves its type. Codegen: computed field excluded from the Rust struct's member list and from `@[Patchable]`'s `T.Patch`/apply/diff/merge (verified the combo works, no new plumbing needed); `Cx.computed_fields` + a `LowerEnv.self_owner` field (self's own env type is `None` by design, so `self.field` needed a different owner-lookup than `x.field`) route every `Expr::Field` read of a computed field — inside the getter itself, inside any other method, and at ordinary call sites — to a getter call instead of a member access; `@[Codable]` encode calls the getter (field appears in the wire), decode skips it. Formatter round-trips `=> expr`; fmt STABILITY test added. Example examples/features/types/computed_field.jet + golden .out. docs/spec/diagnostics.md + syntax-decisions.md updated. cards.title: Blueprint-class visual editor for Jet (full-fidelity, bidirectional)
cards.body: Owner directive (2026-07-02): a FULLY functional Blueprint-style visual editor for Jet is VERY important, especially since Blueprint will no longer be in UE6 — an open market gap Jet can fill. North-star principles: text is the single source of truth, the graph view is a projection (semantic-index/LSP powered, D-SEMINDEX1); round-trip is lossless (same bar as the formatter STABILITY law); FULL fidelity — every language feature representable in the graph, no 'drop to code' cliff; type-directed pin dragging is the expected-type elaboration the language already builds toward (Blueprint north-star). Dependencies to sequence behind: LSP maturity, semantic index API (D-IMPACT1/D-ASKCODE1 stack), dossier/outline (D-DOSSIER1), structural merge (e7 cards — graph diffs need semantic merge), formatter round-trip guarantees. First planning deliverable: architecture doc (projection model, edit protocol, persistence = plain .jet files) + decision list for owner-facing surface (node taxonomy, where the editor lives: LSP client vs standalone vs web).

cards.body: Surfaced by #105: D-MIGRATE1/2 ship compile-time intent checks (E0910) only — codegen erases migration{} blocks, so old-shaped stored data fails decode instead of migrating, and decode_traced (D-MIGRATE3=A) can never report migrated=true. cards.title: Memory model v5: the borrow checker, humanized (D-MEM1)
cards.body: Owner reset 2026-07-03 after four rejected explorations: KEEP Rust borrow-checker semantics; fix ergonomics/beginner experience. v5: three sigils (bare=read default — signatures cannot lie; &=write; ^=take; both mirrored at calls), second-class borrows (no stored/returned raw borrows -> lifetime syntax cannot exist; struct<'a> infection unrepresentable), view values for Str/List slices (no String/&str dualism), named escape hatches Shared<T>/Pool<T> suggested by teaching diagnostics, moves always visible at the ^ site. Deletes ~, D-CAP8 elevation/freeze, api:explicit, L0201, D-REF-SHORTHAND1/2, &-as-share. Keeps RAII, copy verb, resources, arenas/uninit/*T/#Unsafe, D-MUTSELF1. Closest proposal yet to existing AccessConvention machinery (rename + deletion, not rebuild). Proposal: docs/proposals/memory-greenfield.md. If owner approves: deliverable #2 = staged migration path from current implementation. ALL memory-model work gated on D-MEM1.

log.text: Stage S9 (final verification gate) PASSED — THE ENTIRE 9-STAGE MEMORY MODEL V5 MIGRATION IS NOW COMPLETE (S1-S9 all shipped). Stage S7 (policy no_alloc) shipped + independently re-verified (orchestrator, clean after cleaning up a real ENOSPC - session accumulated ~500 leftover /tmp/nix-shell.* dirs across dozens of nix develop invocations, filled the 31G tmpfs to 100%, caused 5 genuine engine_dispatch test failures; rm -rf'd them, confirmed clean rerun, will watch disk going forward). Both types built exactly per the 2 ratified mini-ballots: Shared<T> (D-SHARED-API1=A) - Shared.new(x)/.read(f)/.edit(f) closure-scoped locking (Arc<RwLock<T>> internally, cheap-clone handle passes sendability check across tasks.spawn). cards.title: v5 companion syntax decrees (owner-ratified 2026-07-03)
cards.body: Six owner decrees issued during memory-model v5 review; ratified directly, no ballot needed. Greenfield rule: pre-release spellings leave zero trace — old forms are simply not part of the grammar/stdlib and fail as ordinary unknown syntax; no diagnostics reference them. GREENFIELD RULE (owner 2026-07-03): pre-release spellings leave zero trace — no compat shims, no diagnostics mentioning former forms; old spellings simply are not in the grammar/stdlib and fail as ordinary unknown syntax. (1) D-EMPTYLIT1: empty collection literal is [] for list/map/set alike, type-directed; [:] is not part of the grammar. (2) D-OPT-SPELL1: option constructors are Val(x) / None; value(x) and null do not exist; pattern tests are `== Val(n)`. (3) D-LAMBDA-INFER1: bare lambda params legal wherever the type is inferable (m => m.hp > 0); typed form stays for ambiguity. (4) D-TUPLE-DESTRUCT1: tuple-destructuring binding (a, b) := f(); tasks.channel() returns (Sender<T>, Receiver<T>). (5) D-FILES-WRITE1: core.files is THE file module (no core.fs; users may alias); handle method is .write. (6) D-STR-AFTER1: String gains .after(sep) (+ .before family, exact set minted at impl). Implementation: parser/sema/stdlib + examples + fmt round-trip + ui/golden snapshots + syntax-decisions.md rows + Syntax.rs I7 entries where new tokens. Independent of D-MEM1 sequencing.

cards.title: jet dev (fn-dev web mode) serves 404 for /app.js — pre-existing bug
cards.body: Discovered 2026-07-04 while verifying cv5syntaxdecrees (confirmed pre-existing via git stash to db62a784, unrelated to that card's changes). tests/web_dev.rs::jet_dev_runs_user_defined_dev_fn_and_rebuilds_on_save fails deterministically: GET /app.js returns 404 (expected 200) against a fn dev() server started via devserver.for_app(...).serve(). Fails fast (~0.01-0.02s), meaning the dev server comes up and answers /__jet_dev_version fine, but /app.js routing/build isn't wired or the web build isn't completing before serving. Needs root-cause: check crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs's for_app/serve flow and whatever triggers the web-target build+route registration for app.js.

log.text: Fixed and verified. Root cause was test harness fragility, not devserver routing: the fn-dev tests used fixed ports 8181/8182 and wait_for_server_up accepted any response from /__jet_dev_version, so a stale unrelated server could make the test proceed and then /app.js returned 404. Hardened tests to allocate ephemeral localhost ports and require a 200 version response before proceeding. Verified with nix develop -c cargo test --test web_dev (3/3 pass).

Filed during cv5syntaxdecrees verification. Reproduced deterministically 3x in isolation; confirmed pre-existing on db62a784 (before any v5 syntax decree work) via git stash. Not blocking any current card's checkpoint since it predates them, but real user-facing bug in jet dev's fn-dev web mode.

questions.text: I don’t like any of the names, give me more options, especially that start with Jet or aren’t as themed
questions.answer:
New menu. Jet-prefixed (keeps the family visible on the box):
- Jetport — real word: an airport for jets. "The place your jet lives and launches from" = exactly what the OS is to the language. Short, concrete, easy to say.
- Jetway — the bridge that connects people to the jet. OS as the bridge between you and the machine. Common noun, low collision risk.
- Jetbase — home base for everything jet. Blunt and clear; reads instantly as a platform.
- Jetfield — airfield made ours. Calm, spacious, boots-on-ground feel.
- Jetdeck — the deck everything launches from (carrier deck). Snappy, consumer-friendly.
- Jetcore — reads as "the OS at the core of the jet stack". Generic-ish but strong.
- Jetfoil — real vehicle (hydrofoil jet ferry); fast + sleek connotation, very unclaimed.
- Jetstrip — airstrip; minimal runway an aircraft needs = minimal OS a machine needs.

Less themed / plain words (still fit, don't shout aviation):
- Runway — what everything takes off from. Ordinary word, huge headline appeal ("built on Runway"). Note: Runway ML exists (AI video) — different space but a real collision.
- Hangar — where machines are kept, serviced, configured. Declarative "machine config lives here" energy.
- Tarmac — the ground layer everything sits on. Gritty, memorable, essentially unclaimed in OS space.
- Apron — the paved ground area where aircraft park and load; quiet, unusual, very ownable.
- Groundcrew — the crew that keeps every aircraft ready; fits the "OS does the maintenance for you" story.
- Keel — the spine a vessel is built on; not aviation but same "everything rests on it" role, four letters.

Previous round (still on the table): jetos (safe, generic), Airframe, Jetstream (NATS collision), Flightdeck.

If you want my pick: Jetport first (name says platform-for-jets in one word), Tarmac second (best of the plain-word set). Ballot stays open for your pick — product name is yours.

questions.text: By default I think A is fine, but you should be able to point it to another file so you can have focused files -> I could move the package build to build.jet when it gets too big and it’s easily findable
questions.answer:
You already have exactly that in A — this is the point of the design. Only the name pack.jet is reserved (the identity anchor the tool looks for). Every role (env.*, system.*, fleet.*, build) is a named module declaration, and find() discovers declarations, not filenames. So when pack.jet gets too big you cut the build module out and paste it into build.jet (or packaging/build.jet, or anything) — no pointer, no include line, no config. The tool finds it because of what it DECLARES, not where it lives. Filenames stay 100% your organizational choice; you never have to tell the tool where you moved something.

Ratifying A with this spelled out in the ratification note so the implementation plan makes "role modules may live in any file" an explicit acceptance test.

U20 implementation plan (D-JPK-ADAPTER1=A, D-JPK-ADAPTNAME1=A):

1. Spec/doc cleanup: update docs/spec/spec.md and epoch-4 plan docs so `Pkg.adapt` + `Recipe.prebuilt/copy/cargo/go/node/cmake/make/build` are current law, not pending ballot text. Keep D-JPK-ADAPTNAME1 in syntax-decisions as the source of syntax truth.

2. Env/module evaluation: teach the typed env package evaluator to recognize `Pkg.adapt(...)` entries inside `packages:`. Capture an `AdapterPlan` with name, source provider ref, deps, recipe kind, recipe args, and source span. Reject malformed adapter fields with existing Jetpack diagnostic style and fresh E12xx only if E1236-E1238 do not fit.

3. Recipe surface: map `Recipe.prebuilt(...)` and `Recipe.copy(...)` onto `Jetpack::Recipe::BuildRecipe` first, then add curated build recipes (`cargo`, `go`, `node`, `cmake`, `make`) as thin BuildRecipe constructors over declared tool deps. `Recipe.build(fn(BuildContext))` remains the expert form only when the BuildContext function path can be represented honestly; no placeholder accepted syntax.

4. Realization: extend provider/core realization so adapter packages fetch/stage the source, run the recipe sandbox, install only under the output root, compute output hash, and record store metadata. Lock identity includes source hash/ref, recipe text/hash, helper version, platform, declared tool deps, and output hash.

5. CLI: implement `jet add <ref> --adapt` / `jetpack add <ref> --adapt` as a read-only probe that drafts a concrete `Pkg.adapt(...)` snippet for obvious prebuilt/copy/cargo/go/node/cmake/make cases. It must never run upstream code during probe. Ambiguous/no metadata gets a clear diagnostic naming the manual `Pkg.adapt` path.

6. Tests: add module-eval tests for `Pkg.adapt` capture, recipe unit tests for lock identity and sandbox failures, CLI tests for `--adapt` draft output, and end-to-end offline fixture tests proving prebuilt/copy adapters realize and run from the hangar. Full workspace suite required before done; if unrelated existing failures remain, log exact isolated reproducer.

U21 plan: channel refs and outdated

Decision: D-JPK-CHANNEL1=A is ratified. No owner decision needed. Implement #latest, #main, #v0.x in source-ref positions; resolve only on first add/update; lock records exact identity; realize/build/env never silently re-resolve; jet outdated is read-only; CI or offline with unlocked channel is an error.

Build order:
1. Add channel model in crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/RefSpec.rs and provider-ref parsing helpers: exact ref vs ChannelRef { latest, main, semver mask }. Keep CLI package refs as <source>:<package>.
2. Extend lock identity in crates/jet-driver/src/Lock.rs and crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/WorkspaceLock.rs: store channel intent plus exact resolved rev/tag/hash; parse legacy locks.
3. Split provider resolution mode in crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/Provider.rs: InitialAddOrUpdate may probe remote metadata and move locks; Realize/Build/Env must use exact lock entries.
4. Add jetpack update and jetpack outdated in crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/CLI.rs; register verbs in crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs; route top-level jet update/outdated through Source/EngineDispatch.rs / Source/main.rs if needed.
5. Add CI/offline guard before any channel lookup. A channel ref without exact lock under CI or --offline emits unlocked-channel-in-ci and exits user-error.
6. Update docs/spec/spec.md and docs/spec/diagnostics.md; avoid stale E09xx placeholders.

Likely touched: RefSpec.rs, Provider.rs, CLI.rs, Lock.rs, WorkspaceLock.rs, Syntax.rs, Source/main.rs, Source/EngineDispatch.rs, docs/spec/spec.md, docs/spec/diagnostics.md, tests/jetpack.rs plus module unit tests.

Decision status: D-JPK-DISCOVER1=A is ratified. No owner decision needed.

Build order:
1. Define the local discovery index schema: package source, canonical name, aliases only as typo hints, versions, resolved identity, platforms, docs, option fields, defaults, and provenance. Store as std-only JSONL or compact text under `.jet/` or hangar metadata; no compiler external crates.
2. Populate the index from the same provider metadata used by resolution: core/default packages, registry index entries, locked packages, adapters, service catalog, env/module option descriptors. Do not fetch during `jet search` or `jet info`.
3. Add CLI verbs through the engine dispatch surface: `jet search <query>` and `jet info <ref>`, with `--json` stable shape. Use offline index only; if no local index exists, explain how to create or refresh it.
4. Wire diagnostics and suggestions so unknown package refs can consult the index for nearest names, preserving current E09xx/E12xx style.
5. Add LSP hooks: completions after provider dots inside `module env.*` package lists; completions and hover for typed fields in `Service.{}` and env/module option bodies; hover uses the same index records as CLI.
6. Document discovery as local/offline and tie it to U29: search/info never phones home.

- New `crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/Discovery.rs` or index submodule.
- `crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/{Provider,RefSpec,PackageManifest,ModuleEval/Types,ModuleEval/Diagnostics,Services,CLI}.rs`

- `Source/LSP/{Features,Server}.rs` and LSP fixtures.

- Add E12xx for missing local discovery index and malformed/stale index if needed; every code gets docs and snapshot or pinned process output.

1. Unit-test index write/read, ordering, typo distance, platform filters, and legacy malformed-index failure.

4. LSP fixtures: completion after `default.post`, hover for package refs, completion/hover in `Service.{}` fields.
5. Offline guard: install a provider fixture that would fail if asked for network; `search` and `info` must pass.

cards.plan:
Decision status: D-JPK-BUILDDBG1=A is ratified. No owner decision needed.

Build order:
1. Define a build attempt record: package/ref, source identity, recipe hash, platform, tool deps, step list, start/end status, scratch dir, log dir, and envelope link. Persist under `.jet/logs/build/` or hangar metadata using std-only serialization.
2. Wrap every package/adaptor build step in a runner that captures stdout/stderr per step, records command/env/cwd, timestamps, exit status, and redacts secret values. Successful scratch follows U22 cleanup; failed scratch is preserved under hangar-scoped failure storage.
3. Add `--shell-on-fail` to realize-class verbs that can build packages. On failure, open the configured shell in the preserved scratch with exact PATH/env and cwd at the failed step. In tests, allow a fake shell command so no interactive test hangs.
4. Extend `jet explain <ref>` without breaking diagnostic-code `jet explain E1234`: code-shaped args keep existing behavior; package/ref args print resolution path, provider choice, lock identity, recipe/provenance, last build status, failed step, and log path.
5. Add `jet logs <pkg>` with text and `--json`; include per-step logs, latest/attempt selection, and stable JSON schema for CI.
6. Wire the primary build-failure diagnostic to name the failed step, `jet logs <pkg>`, and `--shell-on-fail`.

- `crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/{Recipe,Provider,Store,Envelope,RefSpec,CLI,Shell,JSON}.rs`

1. Unit-test attempt record read/write and redaction.
2. Fixture adapter with three steps where step 2 fails: assert scratch preserved, log files written, diagnostic names step 2 and fix commands.

4. `jet explain weirdctl` after failure prints provider path, source hash, recipe hash, platform, failed step, scratch, log path.

cards.title: Highlighting: one source of truth across editors
cards.body: Audit 2026-07-05: three hand-kept grammars drift — vscode tmLanguage 164 lines, tree-sitter 998, zed highlights.scm 136, vs 569 registered tokens in Syntax.rs (I7). The v5 'copy' verb (shipped S4) is highlighted in NO grammar; VS Code, Zed, and GitHub color the same file differently. Owner: 'even code highlighting doesnt seem consistent.' Decision D-HL1.
cards.plan:
Highlighting single source of truth under D-HL1=D (grammars generated from Syntax.rs + LSP semantic-token overlay, CI drift gate). Implement on master. Invariant I7: Syntax.rs is already the registry every user-typeable token must live in — this card makes that fact enforce coloring.

Build order:
1. Classify the registry: extend crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs entries with a highlight class per token (keyword.control / keyword.declaration / keyword.ownership / marker / operator / sigil / literal-prefix ...). Mechanical: a const table or attribute alongside each existing entry; no token strings move. Any token without a class = compile error in the generator, so future ratifications can't skip it.
2. Generator: `jet devtools grammars` in Source/CmdDevTools.rs. Emits BEGIN/END GENERATED sections inside: editors/vscode/syntaxes/jet.tmLanguage.json (keyword/marker/operator patterns), editors/tree-sitter/grammar.js keyword externals (or a generated keywords.js the grammar requires), editors/zed/languages/jet/highlights.scm keyword block. Hand-written structure rules (strings, comments, interpolation, blocks) stay outside the markers and are preserved byte-for-byte on regeneration. Generator is deterministic (sorted output) so regeneration is diff-stable.
3. Drift gate: tests/grammar.rs gains every_syntax_token_is_highlighted — for each user-typeable token in Syntax.rs, assert presence in each grammar's generated section, and assert the generated sections match a fresh in-memory generation (stale-file detection). Red today (copy, ^, & missing) until stage 2 output is committed. This test joins the CI PR gate (#211).
4. Semantic overlay: extend Source/LSP semantic tokens — add token types/modifiers for v5 ownership (& write-borrow, ^ move, copy verb), markers (#Test/#Unsafe/... as decorator-class), retired/foreign keywords (E03xx teaching-error spellings) explicitly NOT keyword-colored. editors/vscode/package.json semanticTokenScopes maps the new types; zed extension.toml equivalents. questions.text: Propose a potential hybrid solution that carefully combines the best of each. What do unreal and unity and godot do? What are the downsides of each approach? What do most game developers prefer? What is the best option? How can we mitigate/fix the downsides of your proposed option?
questions.answer: Hybrid proposal: choose a refined C: scene-first + component scripts + frame hook + optional systems. Shape: `Scene` is durable editable data, nodes/entities own sprites/colliders/audio/input bindings, behavior attaches as small scripts/components, and `scene.on_frame` remains the one-file beginner escape hatch. Later, high-scale code can add ECS-style systems over the same scene data; that is an expert layer, not the first tutorial. What major engines do: Unreal centers placed Actors with Components and Blueprints/C++ behavior; Unity centers GameObjects in Scenes with Components/MonoBehaviour callbacks; Godot centers a tree of Nodes saved as Scenes with scripts and per-frame callbacks. All three converge on the same product truth: visual/editor-readable scene data plus attached behavior. Downsides: callback-only is easiest but gives the visual editor no durable model; app-object is tidy code but still not naturally visual; scene-first can hide lifecycle order and get stringly/inspector-heavy; ECS-first scales but is too abstract for first-week users. Most game developers, especially Unity/Godot/Unreal users, prefer object/scene/component workflows for day-to-day creation; engine/performance specialists like ECS underneath, but not as the beginner surface. Best option: C, amended into the hybrid above. Mitigations: code-first scene declarations must round-trip into the editor; names/asset refs get typed handles not raw strings where possible; lifecycle has one clear order (`init`, `on_frame`, physics if present, draw); ECS/query APIs are available behind `core.game.systems` for advanced scale; the first tutorial still fits in one file and never says “component query” before a ball moves. Sources checked: official Unity GameObject docs, Godot Nodes and Scenes docs, Unreal Actor/Component docs.

cards.title: HTTPS by default in core.http
cards.body: core.net/core.http default build is plain-HTTP; https needs opt-in core.tls (jet-net: 'HTTPS requires a TLS feature; the default build is HTTP-only'). Nearly every real API is https — first-week beginners hit this wall. Decision D-TLS1: how TLS becomes default (vendored rustls bridge -> native post-E3, system TLS, or status quo).
cards.plan:
HTTPS by default under D-TLS1=A: rustls in the default build via the I6 FFI-bridge pattern, certificate verification pinned to system trust roots, native Jet TLS post-E3 only behind an external security-audit gate. Implement on master. Invariants: I2 (every TLS failure is a Jet-voiced diagnostic — rustls/OS error text never reaches the user raw), I4 (every new diagnostic gets a code + what/why/fix + ui snapshot), I6 (rustls rides the bridge like wasmtime/age precedents — D-DEP-CRYPTO1 governance, not a compiler dep).

Build order:
1. jet-net grows a default-on TLS path: rustls + system trust roots (rustls-native-certs-class) behind the existing fetch API in crates/jet-net; ureq's tls feature wired accordingly. Default build = https works; a no-tls build flag remains for freestanding/size-gated targets (release_gates.rs budgets re-checked — if the size budget breaks, that goes back to the owner as a question, not a silent budget bump).
2. core.http / core.net client: https URLs work in `jet run` with zero manifest. The E-code path 'https needs core.tls' dies for the client; core.tls package remains for advanced config (pinning, client certs, custom roots) per option A's decided scope.
3. Server side: extend the #17 HTTP server surface with TLS serving — API shape follows the existing ratified server surface (.tls(cert, key) style continuation of the #17 mandate; if the shape needs anything beyond a method on the existing builder, STOP and ballot it — do not invent surface).
4. Diagnostics (product copy, snapshot-pinned): new E42xx family — certificate invalid/expired/hostname mismatch, handshake failure, no trust roots found (the minimal-container case: name the fix — install ca-certificates), protocol errors. Each: docs/spec/diagnostics.md entry, jet explain page, tests/ui snapshot. The front end translates every rustls error class; an untranslated class panicking through = P0 per I2.
5. Tests without network: local test server with self-signed + valid-chain fixtures under tests/fixtures (generate once, check in; regeneration script documented); happy-path https fetch, each E42xx provoked deliberately. CI never touches the internet.
6. Example: examples/features/net/https_fetch.jet against the fixture server (env-pointed base URL so the example text reads like the real world but the test stays hermetic); golden-tested (I5).
7. Record the security gate: release-policy.md gains the D-TLS1 clause — native-TLS may replace rustls as default only after external audit + interop battery (vs rustls and OpenSSL test vectors); syntax-decisions.md logs D-TLS1=A in the stdlib section; roadmap.md deferred-registry paragraph updated (TLS line now says https default via rustls bridge).

questions.text: What are the tradeoffs of having two separate constructors vs passing in tls as an option? Go seems to be the best in class in general -> what does community sentiment say? What do the vast majority of professionals prefer?
questions.answer: Tradeoff: separate constructors (`serve` + `serve_tls`) are extremely discoverable and match Go surface style, but they fork the API every time a new transport/config appears (`serve_h2`, `serve_unix`, `serve_mtls`, etc.). A `tls:` option keeps one server entry point and composes with future options, but can decay into a bag of knobs unless options are typed and named. Go sentiment: Go is respected because the easy path is tiny, but serious services usually graduate from convenience functions to an `http.Server`/`Transport` config object; Go docs show both: `ListenAndServe`/`ListenAndServeTLS` for convenience, custom `Server` for control, and custom `Transport` for TLS/proxy/etc. Vast-majority professional preference is not “many constructors forever”; it is “one obvious simple path, plus typed config when real deployment needs it.” Recommendation: keep D-TLSSERVE1=A, possibly sharpen it as hybrid-A: `Server.serve(addr, mux)` for plaintext and `Server.serve(addr, mux, tls: Server.tls(cert,key))` for HTTPS, with `tls` a typed option object that can later carry mTLS/client-auth/ALPN without new verbs. Mitigation: only allow a small fixed set of named options, reject unlabeled positional TLS, and document C/Go-style separate `serve_tls` as intentionally not chosen because it multiplies verbs as server config grows. Sources checked: Go net/http docs for convenience functions + custom Server/Transport.

cards.body: Update jetpack run package to show clearly that a package is running/was run. When running cowsay with no input args, looked like jetpack shell was frozen
cards.plan:
#215 plan: make jetpack run package visibility obvious

Decision: no owner decision needed. Owner reported that running cowsay with no input args looked like a frozen jetpack shell. This is output/UX polish inside existing run-package behavior, not new syntax.

Build order:
1. Identify explicit package-run path in crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/CLI.rs cmd_run. Today explicit ref plus no -- command falls through to Shell::enter, which can look frozen. Keep project-env run with no explicit ref as shell entry, but for explicit package refs run the package binary by default or print an unmistakable banner before shell entry. Preferred: explicit jetpack run nixpkgs:cowsay with no -- runs cowsay, matching top-level jet run lowering.
2. Add visible lifecycle output around package execution. Before Shell::run_command, print status to stderr via Output::Theme: running <ref> -> <binary> and note when args are empty. If useful, print finished <binary> with exit code on stderr after child exits. Never write status to stdout.
3. Preserve script behavior: respect --no-color/NO_COLOR, preserve child exit status exactly, avoid duplicate banners, and avoid post-run noise that breaks stdout golden tests.
4. Top-level parity: Source/main.rs dispatch_nixpkgs_run lowers jet run nixpkgs:<tool> to jetpack run nixpkgs:<tool> -- <tool>. Ensure visibility appears for direct jetpack run and top-level jet run without duplicate status.
5. Update docs only if explicit-ref no-command semantics change from shell-enter to default-run. Add tests around no-arg package execution and blocking commands.

Likely touched: crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/CLI.rs, Jetpack/Shell.rs if lifecycle belongs beside run_command, Jetpack/Output.rs for helper if needed, Source/main.rs only for duplicate suppression, tests/jetpack.rs, CLI transcript snapshots, docs/spec/spec.md if command contract changes.

questions.text: Give me tradeoffs of [List] and [Map, MapVal] style shorthands for the two most common types, but then the consistent rust style List<Type> for more specific collection types (HashMap<Type>, etc)
questions.answer: Tradeoff: shorthand for the two dominant containers keeps daily Jet light (`[User]`, map shorthand), while Rust-style named generics keep specific collection policy visible (`HashMap<K, V>`, `Deque<T>`). Main risk is two generic-looking systems: brackets for defaults, angle brackets for named structures. For map shorthand specifically, comma form `[K, V]` is compact but reads like a pair/tuple; colon form `[K: V]` better says key maps to value and matches map literals. I updated the ballot with both the hybrid recommendation and the exact comma-style variant as a separate option.

questions.text: What would we need to create a first class exceptional event system? Something that would be a great fit in game dev with the ability to subscribe to events, have hooks, would be great for web dev, etc.
questions.answer:
Yes. A first-class Jet event system should be its own runtime/framework feature, then Canvas projects it as Blueprint-style event graphs. The shape I would build is a typed Event<T> / Hook<T> model with four layers: (1) event declarations are ordinary Jet values or framework-owned callback slots with typed payload structs; (2) subscription returns a disposable/cancellable handle tied to owner lifetime, so game objects, UI components, and web handlers cannot leak; (3) dispatch has explicit phase/order policy: before/after/around hooks, priority only where deterministic ordering matters, once/debounce/throttle helpers as library adapters, and a clear sync vs async dispatch split; (4) failures are typed: handlers can be infallible, fallible, or cancelling, and the publisher chooses collect/log/stop-on-first-error semantics in the event type.

For game dev this gives input, collision, lifecycle, tick/frame, animation, physics, and gameplay messages. For web dev it gives DOM-like interaction events, lifecycle hooks, data-change signals, navigation, server request hooks, and reactive UI updates. For systems/server code it gives lifecycle, plugin hooks, telemetry, scheduler, and hot-reload events.

Required pieces before it is real: a std/runtime event library, typed subscription handles, lifecycle ownership rules, structured-concurrency integration, backpressure/queue policy for async events, deterministic ordering rules, diagnostics for dead subscriptions/reentrant dispatch/bad async handlers, debugger trace support, and Canvas projection/write transactions.

Best hybrid: ratify Canvas event graphs as views over ordinary callback/event functions now, then create a separate first-class Event/Hook design card for E3/E6 runtime work. Do not invent event Foo syntax inside Canvas. Let the event system be one canonical semantic model usable from source, Canvas, game dev, web dev, and server hooks.

questions.text: I'm not 100% sure what this means in practice. I also dont know that I like the "provider" term, consider better fitting options & update accordingly with tradeoffs and direct comparisons to how other systems/software handles this, then present me the best no compromises hybrid solution
questions.answer: Updated D-CANVAS-EXT2. Short answer: yes, use the existing Jet JIT for Canvas run/preview and sandboxed package Canvas actions. No separate Canvas runtime/compiler. New terms: palette entry = read-only projected Jet function/type metadata; Canvas action = behavior-producing Jet function that can propose edits/previews; external adapter = opt-in native/tool bridge. Best hybrid is option B: Canvas invokes checked Jet action code through executable TIR/JIT, accepts only returned source transactions/previews, then formatter+sema revalidates and logs package id/version/hash, authority, touched files, diff, and diagnostics. AOT stays build/export path. Direct comparisons added for Blueprint, VS Code, Rust proc macros, and Figma/Blender plugins.

cards.title: corelib audit: core.time ring — calendar parity with java.time/jiff
cards.body:
Best-in-class bar: java.time (JSR-310) semantics and jiff (Rust) correctness. Card #53 (time depth) is done — first verify what actually shipped, then close residual gaps.

Audit list: civil Date / Time / DateTime types distinct from the ms timestamp; ZonedDateTime with a bundled, updatable IANA tzdb (DST-correct arithmetic — the thing most languages get wrong); Duration vs calendar Period distinction; RFC 3339 / ISO 8601 parse + format; custom format patterns; monotonic Instant separate from wall clock (Stopwatch exists — expose the primitive); truncate/round to unit; day-of-week/ordinal/week-based math; leap-second policy stated in docs; conversion to/from Unix ms without ambiguity traps.

Done means: the documented ring surface provably covers the JSR-310 core use-case table, with examples + golden tests per area. Ballot gates: any new user-facing module name, function surface, or syntax is an owner decision (queue ballots before code); any external dep stays behind the FFI bridge pattern (I6).

cards.title: jetos: declarative VM integration-test framework (NixOS test-driver parity)
cards.body:
The NixOS VM test framework is its most-lauded infrastructure — jetos needs a better one to claim drop-in-and-better. Scope: declare a multi-host scenario in Jet (system.<host> configs + a typed test script — not strings driving Python like NixOS), orchestrate QEMU guests from the #263 harness, typed assertions (unit active, port open, file content, command output), inter-VM networking, deterministic replay + proof artifacts, failure output in Jet's diagnostic voice.

Beat-NixOS axes: typed test script with sema-checked host/service references (a typo'd service name fails at compile time), and first-class artifact/provenance capture. Builds on #262/#263 — coordinate with the jetos agent; this is a new layer, not their installer/system-core scope.
cards.plan:
Plan refreshed 2026-07-07 by codex-main.

Ratified decisions:
- D-JOS-VMTEST1=A: Hybrid: vmtest declarations as test targets. Top-level vmtest.<name> declarations are the canonical scenario surface, and the same object is also a normal test target for CI, filtering, artifacts, and package integration. cards.title: jetos: module option priorities, overrides, and module disabling (mkDefault/mkForce parity)
cards.body:
Owner's config uses lib.mkForce (disable SDDM on the plasma-beta variant), lib.mkDefault (stateVersion), disabledModules (stylix kmscon), and system tags. NixOS solves multi-module option conflict with numeric priorities nobody can explain; jetos must solve it better or the module system can't compose real configs.

Scope: a ratified conflict/priority story for options set by multiple modules — default vs normal vs force tiers with typed spellings; disabling an imported module wholesale; per-variant overrides (one host, variants overriding single options); generation tags/labels; and the explain surface — "what set this value, what lost, why" wired into #323 options search. This is core module-system semantics: ballot the surface before code (D-JOS pattern). Coordinate with jetos agent's #262 module schema.

Best-in-class bar: Rust tracing (spans) + Go slog (simplicity) + OpenTelemetry (export). core.log shipped in Epoch 2 — audit the real surface first.

Audit list: leveled structured fields with typed values (not string-formatted); runtime level filtering per module; span/scope context that propagates across core.tasks spawns; sinks — stderr human format, file, JSON lines; rotation policy; sampling for high-volume paths; OTLP/OpenTelemetry export (bridge gate if any dep); metrics floor (counter/gauge/histogram) or an explicit decision that metrics is its own module (ballot); print vs log guidance in docs.

Done means: audit table plus shipped gaps with examples + golden tests; a service example emits parseable JSON logs with spans across tasks. Ballot gates: any new user-facing module name, function surface, or syntax is an owner decision (queue ballots before code); any external dep stays behind the FFI bridge pattern (I6).

cards.title: corelib audit: collections + iterator adapters — parity with Rust Iterator/itertools
cards.body:
Best-in-class bar: Rust's Iterator trait — the most-lauded iterator design anywhere — plus Python itertools breadth. Set/Deque shipped (#55).

Container gaps: sorted map/sorted set (BTree-class, ordered iteration); binary heap / priority queue; LRU cache; bitset; growable byte buffer with endian-aware read/write (Reader exists for consuming — the building half is missing).

Iterator/sequence adapter audit — one canonical spelling each (I8): enumerate, zip/unzip, windows, chunks, flat_map, filter_map, take_while/skip_while, fold/reduce/scan, dedup, partition, group-by/chunk-by, min_by/max_by/min_by_key, sort_by_key, counts/frequency map, sum/product over selectors, first/last/nth, any/all (verify), flatten, intersperse/join beyond strings. Whatever list-comprehension/pipeline surface exists must reach the same operations without a second mechanism.

Done means: audit table in docs; gaps shipped with examples + golden tests; the doc shows the canonical Jet spelling next to the Rust/Python name so migrants find it instantly. Ballot gates: any new user-facing module name, function surface, or syntax is an owner decision (queue ballots before code); any external dep stays behind the FFI bridge pattern (I6).
cards.plan:
Plan refreshed 2026-07-07 by codex-main.

- D-ITERTOOLS1=A: Hybrid: lazy iterator protocol with eager collection conveniences. One Iterable/Iterator model powers lazy adapters. Collections expose beginner-friendly adapter methods that return lazy views; `collect`, `to_list`, or terminal reducers make materialization explicit. No comprehension syntax needed now.

Ready state: Owner gates clear; card is ready for implementation.

cards.title: Workspace re-partition: shrink jet-driver, make placeholder crates real or fold them
cards.body:
jet-driver is ~44k lines and has absorbed three products: the compiler driver, Jetpack (Jetpack/CLI.rs ~4.5k, package engine), and JetOS (Jetpack/JetOS.rs ~7.2k). Meanwhile four workspace crates are shells: jet-queries (375 lines), jet-rt (401), jet-net (295), jet-impact (314). Epoch 4 (jetpack) and Epoch 7 (jetos) will grow these surfaces substantially — re-partition before they grow, not after.

Scope:
1. Extract Jetpack and JetOS out of jet-driver into their own crates (jet-pack / jet-os or per ratified naming canon: jetpack engine, jetos). jet-driver keeps only compile-pipeline orchestration + CLI dispatch.
2. For each shell crate decide: become real now, or fold into its owner until needed. jet-queries is the big one — it is the incremental-compilation seam; decide whether the query architecture becomes load-bearing now (retrofitting incrementality into a 268k-line compiler later is strictly worse). Produce a recommendation with the decision reasoning recorded in architecture.md.
3. Update docs/spec/architecture.md: crate map, dependency direction rules, which crate owns which pipeline stage (R1–R12 mapping).
4. Enforce direction: no back-edges (e.g. codegen must not depend on driver). Add a workspace-level check if cheap (cargo tree assertions in a test).

Strictly behavior-preserving: zero user-visible change, golden/snapshot suites byte-identical, full suite green. No owner gates expected (no user-facing syntax); if extraction forces a user-visible rename anywhere, ballot first. Sequencing note: do this card before the monster-file decomposition card touches Jetpack/JetOS/CLI files, so those files move once, not twice.
cards.plan: Order: (1) map current jet-driver module graph + who imports what (rg + cargo tree); (2) write the target crate map as a short architecture.md draft section — get it reviewed in-repo before moving code; (3) extract JetOS first (most self-contained), then Jetpack engine, then CLI dispatch cleanup — one extraction per commit, full suite green between each; (4) shell-crate verdicts: implement or fold, one commit each; (5) jet-queries decision writeup (incrementality now vs later) — this is a design recommendation, not a gate: record in architecture.md; (6) final pass: dependency-direction test, docs updated, full nix develop -c cargo test green.

cards.title: Decompose monster files: CoreLib.rs, Canvas.rs, TIR lower/emit, CheckerCoreLib.rs, JetOS.rs
cards.body:
Largest files today: crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib.rs (13.5k lines), Source/Canvas.rs (8.4k), crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/lower.rs (8.3k), crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib.rs (7.5k), crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/JetOS.rs (7.2k), Parser/Items.rs (5.7k), TIR/emit.rs (5.3k), TIR/subset.rs (5.1k), CheckerInfer/calls.rs (4.8k), Jetpack/CLI.rs (4.5k), jet-jit/src/lib.rs (4.5k). These files burn agent context every session and are where merge mistakes concentrate. Style rule already says small modules — enforce it.

Scope: semantics-preserving decomposition of every file above ~3k lines into responsibility-named submodules. Seams follow responsibility, not line count — e.g. CoreLib.rs splits by core module family (files/io/net/…), lower.rs by TIR construct family, CheckerCoreLib.rs mirroring the CoreLib split so sema and codegen stay navigable in parallel. Target ≤ ~1,500 lines per file; judgment allowed where a real unit resists splitting — record why in the commit message.

Rules: pure code motion — no renames of public items, no behavior change, no drive-by refactors. Safety net is the existing suite: golden outputs and UI snapshots must be byte-identical; full suite green after every file's decomposition (one file per commit). Sequencing: JetOS.rs, CLI.rs, and Canvas.rs only AFTER the workspace re-partition card lands, so they move across crates once, not twice; start with CoreLib.rs / lower.rs / CheckerCoreLib.rs / Items.rs, which the re-partition does not touch.

Done means: no source file above the target without a recorded justification; module maps make sense from names alone; zero snapshot diffs; full nix develop -c cargo test green. No owner gates.
cards.plan: Order: (1) CoreLib.rs — split by core.* family, mod.rs keeps the registration table; (2) CheckerCoreLib.rs — mirror the same family split; (3) TIR lower.rs then emit.rs then subset.rs — split by construct family (items, exprs, patterns, control flow, closures, tasks); (4) Parser/Items.rs + CheckerInfer/calls.rs; (5) jet-jit/src/lib.rs; (6) wait for re-partition card, then JetOS.rs, Jetpack/CLI.rs, Canvas.rs inside their new homes. Per file: read wholly first, write the module map, mechanical motion, cargo test --test golden + targeted suites, one commit; full suite at card close.
