cards.title: Tier-0 deopt target runs only a pure subset, so jet run fails where jet build succeeds
cards.body:
D-LENS-RUN2=A says missing tier-1 coverage deopts per function to the canonical tier-0 interpreter with identical observable behavior. It does not hold. The tier-0 target is the comptime evaluator, which by its own diagnostic evaluates only a pure subset of Jet. Any construct Cranelift cannot compile and comptime does not implement fails under default jet run while jet build succeeds.

Two live repros, both exit 0 under jet build and exit 1 under jet run:

examples/features/crypto/crypto_suite.jet — trace shows 'run tier0 interp (body stmt 6: Let[0] init=OtherExpr)', then E0956 'jet.crypto.sha512_bytes() at comptime can't run at compile time yet'.

examples/features/types/generic_constructor_inference.jet — E0956 'static Box.new can't run at compile time yet'. AOT prints '7 jet 2 9'.

The diagnostic text is also wrong for this path. A user who typed jet run is told the work cannot happen at compile time, and is advised to compute the value at runtime, which is what they asked for.

Both examples reached the compile attempt only after frontend fixes landed on 2026-07-28, so the defect was previously masked rather than introduced.
cards.plan: Decide the correct law first: either the tier-0 deopt target must cover every executable construct, or deopt must route to a full runtime interpreter rather than the comptime evaluator. Then close the gap so a program that succeeds under jet build succeeds under default jet run with byte-identical output. Separate the user-facing diagnostic fix: E0956 must not tell a jet run user that their work cannot happen at compile time. blockedBy: none.

cards.title: JIT: ProcessSpec env, env_remove and cwd missing or silently ignored
cards.body:
The JIT host table has no working entry for the argument-taking ProcessSpec builders. `env` and `env_remove` are absent. `jet_jit_process_spec_cwd` exists but silently ignores its argument.

The silent case is the worse one. A program that sets a working directory under `jet run` runs in the wrong directory and reports no error, so the failure surfaces later as a missing file or a wrong result. A missing entry at least fails loudly.

cards.title: Codegen panics during jet check on a sema-rejected program
cards.body:
`jet check` on `ui_fixed_dynamic_size.E0103.jet` reaches `unreachable!()` at crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/lower/method_calls.rs:944 and panics.

Sema reports E0103 correctly, so the program is already rejected. A lowering path still runs afterwards and crashes on it. The user sees a compiler panic instead of the diagnostic that sema already produced.

The underlying question is ordering: why does lowering run at all on a program sema has rejected? That is a design call, not a guess, which is why the worker who found it did not patch it.

questions.text: We are ALWAYS looking to spend more time and effort up front to have a better long term experience, both from a dx perspective, but also to get better performance and ergonomics at the end of the day. What kind of benefits do we get from option C? Since it sounds like it costs more up front but doesnt seem to have other negatives listed does that mean performance is better?
questions.answer:
No. Option C does not make runtime branches faster than option B.

B and C can feed the same middle-end arm-table IR. After that, D-BRANCH-CODEGEN1 (already ratified as B) picks select, match, data table, jump table, or ordered compares. That classifier is where bare-metal wins live.

What C buys instead:

1. One IR from the parser onward. No classic If tree beside Switch arms.
2. No desugar pass that can drift from parse or forget a path.
3. Every future lint, IDE walk, and lowering sees one shape.
4. Long-term simpler compiler DX, at higher up-front parser, formatter, and IDE cost.

What C does not buy:

- Faster user programs than a correct early desugar (B)
- Different user syntax (still one if)

So: spend more up front on C for a cleaner long-term compiler. Spend the performance effort on the classifier and subject binding, which you already locked in CODEGEN1.

I updated D-BRANCH-AST1: option C detail is clearer, and the recommendation now points to C given your up-front investment rule. You can still pick B if you want the smaller first patch with a desugar bridge.

cards.title: Auto-derive defaults: reject and override
cards.body: Pragmatism gap (seed for pragmatism-audit): beginner path should auto-derive useful built-in traits by default; experts need an explicit reject path and a hand override path. Amend or extend S55 / D-MARK-DEBUG1 family so default-on + reject + override is one mechanism.
cards.plan:
Ratified: D-AUTODERIVE1=E — default-on auto-derive, a package-level kill switch, per-type reject, and per-type hand override. One mechanism, three scopes.

1. Keep the S55 silent auto-derive as the default (Printable, Equatable, Debug when every field qualifies).
2. Add the per-type reject path so a type opts out of one derived trait without writing an impl.
3. Keep the hand-written impl as the override. It already wins today; make sure reject and override do not fight.
4. Add the package policy knob. Auto-derive is on by default; a package may turn it off, and inside that package auto-derive becomes opt-in. Type reject and hand override still work there.
5. Syntax chores: Syntax.rs row, syntax-decisions.md log line under S55, regenerate devtools grammars, rebless snapshots.
6. Ship one example that shows all three scopes and the docs entry beside it.

cards.title: HTTP JSON, static directory, and CORS defaults
cards.body: Pragmatism gaps from the 2026-07-28 audit (findings 8 and 14). The most common service jobs re-glue what the stack already knows. (1) JSON: client reads resp.body().text(limit) then decodes separately; server handlers hand-build JSON strings and headers. #Codable already owns typed encode/decode. (2) Static: static_file ships; serving a directory (static_files(root)) is owner-gated open. (3) CORS: a browser front plus Jet API needs hand-rolled OPTIONS and headers. Three ballots on this card: D-HTTP-JSON1, D-HTTP-STATIC-FILES1, D-HTTP-CORS1.
cards.plan:
Three ratified rulings, one slice, one HTTP surface. D-HTTP-JSON1=A, D-HTTP-STATIC-FILES1=A, D-HTTP-CORS1=A.

1. JSON both ways, over the existing #Codable path. Add `resp.json<T>(limit)` on the client, `req.json<T>()` on the server, and `server.json(status, value)` for responses. Each is one Result. `server.json` sets Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8. `req.json<T>()` honours the framing cap already ratified for bodies. The raw text and byte paths stay for experts.
2. `static_files(root)` mounts a directory under a prefix. Defaults: normalize the path, refuse escapes, hide dot-files, refuse symbolic links that leave the root, serve index.html for a directory request or 404. Content types come from the existing mime table. Range requests reuse the shipped per-file machinery. Named options carry index, dotfiles, and follow_links for experts.
3. `server.cors(policy)` middleware. CorsPolicy names origins (a list or .Any), methods, headers, credentials, and max_age. No policy installed means no CORS headers at all. The constructor rejects .Any with credentials and says why. The middleware answers OPTIONS preflight and stamps allow headers on matching routes.
4. Update docs/reference/core-library.md and extend examples/features/net/http_rest_service.jet to use the typed JSON calls, a static mount, and a CORS policy.

Owned paths: the http client and server modules under crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib, docs/reference/core-library.md, examples/features/net/.

Proof: targeted http tests for each of the three; a hostile-path test proving the static mount refuses escapes, dot-files, and link escapes; a constructor test proving .Any plus credentials is rejected; example golden; independent review closes.

questions.text: For webapps in particular, why would this not be jet dev site.jet ? I thought we already set it up so unless dev is overriden & specified further, it will auto serve the app.
questions.answer: You are right that jet dev is the natural home — but the auto-serve you remember does not exist yet. Today jet dev only serves when the file itself defines fn dev() that constructs and runs core.web.devserver, and that devserver serves web-target build artifacts (JS/Wasm/static files), not web.app() routes. Nothing anywhere lowers the app graph onto any server, under any command — that missing lowering is what this ballot authorizes. I added option D matching your model: jet dev site.jet auto-serves the app graph with live reload whenever the entry builds a web.app and no fn dev() overrides it; jet run site.jet serves the same graph without dev extras, because for a server app the running server IS the program (that is also the deployment path). fn dev() and an explicit app.serve(port) stay as the expert overrides. Recommendation moved to D.

questions.text: For apps in particular, the goal is to be able to write it once & have it work everywhere -> web, native(macos, linux, windows), mobile, etc. We want to avoid the need for things like tauri or electron or (flutter?) -> you write it once, it works everywhere. YOU CHOOSE where you deploy, you dont get bent over just trying to keep development in parallel across 3 different client targets
questions.answer: Agreed — and that goal is exactly option B: one ui tree, one on_click, and every backend (GTK today, web, terminal, mobile later) renders it and routes its events. That is the Electron/Tauri killer: no JS shell and no parallel client codebases; you choose the deploy target, the code does not change. B needs real design first (stable node identity across renders on the DOM backend, an event channel from JS into Wasm, the portable event set), which is why the ballot recommended A: it uses only existing surface (web.on + signals) to stop the flagship teaching that JavaScript owns the click. I added option D to make the sequence explicit and ratifiable: land A today, and ratify B as the destination with its own design card — the demo respells to the portable on_click when B lands. D buys the write-once story without leaving the flagship wrong in the meantime. Recommendation moved to D.

Ratified: D-GAME-LOOP1=A — a real backend drives on_frame until the window closes; headless keeps a deterministic frame budget.

4. Make scene.query return component data, not marker strings, so on_frame has something to work with.
5. Extend the raylib bridge example into a real loop with input and audio, so the surface stops implying playability it does not have.

questions.text: for a game loop, wouldnt you just put the loop inside the fn run() {...}? Or fn dev() {...}?
questions.answer: You do — your game code lives in fn run(), and on desktop you could hand-write loop { ... } there today. The loop itself sits behind game.run because the parts that vary per platform belong to the backend: the stop condition (window close vs headless frame budget), frame pacing (vsync / FPS cap), and the input/event pump. And on the web target you cannot write the loop at all — the browser forbids blocking the main thread, so frames must be scheduled as callbacks (requestAnimationFrame). The callback body inside game.run is the only shape that works on desktop, headless CI, and browser alike — the same write-once argument as apps. Option A adds no new mechanism; it fixes the stop condition so the loop game.run already owns runs until the player quits instead of exactly three frames. fn dev() is orthogonal here: it is an alternate entry for dev tooling, not a different loop.

cards.title: Compile-checked literal regex patterns
cards.body: Pragmatism audit 2026-07-28, smaller notes. Every one-shot regex call on a string literal pays a Result plus ?? panic tax (regex.jet:8-28), though the pattern is known at compile time and the engine is linear-time by construction. Ballot: D-REGEX-LIT1.
cards.plan:
Ratified: D-REGEX-LIT1=D — a regex is always a typed literal, and the head is inferable at a pattern-typed argument.

1. Make the one-shot `re.*` pattern parameters take the pattern type. A leading-dot literal `.{"..."}` then resolves against them the way an enum variant shorthand resolves against an expected enum.
2. Sema compile-validates the literal with the linear-engine parser. The diagnostic carries the offset inside the pattern. A validated literal call returns the match directly, with no `??`.
3. `Regex.{"..."}` with the explicit head is the same construct. It works everywhere, and it is how a named reusable pattern value is written.
4. A bare string literal where a pattern is expected is a compile error whose fix text shows the `.{"..."}` form. Register the code and its UI snapshot (I4).
5. Runtime-built patterns keep today's fallible Result signature through the compiled-pattern path. Nothing there changes.
6. Rewrite examples/features/text/regex.jet to teach the literal form first, and refresh the golden.

Owned paths: crates/jet-sema (literal head inference and pattern validation), the core.regex module, crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs, examples/features/text/regex.jet, docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md.

Proof: targeted tests for an inferred head, an explicit head, a bad pattern with the offset in the message, a bare string rejection, and a runtime-built pattern still returning Result; example golden; independent review closes.

log.text: Independent review closed both criteria. Exact reusable Regex parity and both UI proofs passed.

Exact-test fix aa0acc931: comptime fragment lowering now recovers Regex and Match receiver types from canonical global values, so global Regex.match and Match accessor calls lower as handle methods instead of unsupported static calls. The parity fixture now uses distinct comptime and runtime binding names, preserving the same direct-comptime versus runtime assertions without a false global/local collision. Static diff checks passed; root owns the exact test rerun.

Final batch review fix a2620fa4c: direct comptime Regex.replace_all_with now intercepts in the interpreter context and invokes the shared regex replacement helper through the existing inline-closure evaluator. The context-free Builtins path no longer carries an unsupported callback stub. TIR continues to use the same helper through its callable evaluator. Static diff checks passed; grouped tests remain pending.

Batch review fix bfa4e4a6d: TIR Match values now preserve group names and byte spans, and the evaluator implements group, name, start, end, group_start, and group_end. Regex replacement now expands numbered and named captures. replace_all_with stays a RegexMethod and invokes TIR callables through the existing evaluator seam. The forced-comptime-TIR parity regression covers Match accessors, capture replacement, and callback replacement. Static diff checks passed; grouped tests remain pending.

Grouped review fix 05581bb99: the comptime regex executor now consumes the canonical validated grammar and supports noncapturing and named groups, range quantifiers, and Unicode classes. Reusable Regex methods now dispatch through the existing regex core operations, with a comptime/TIR/runtime regression. Static diff check passed; grouped tests remain pending.

Committed as 418e4e5cd feat(regex): add checked typed literals. Worktree is clean. Fresh batch reviewer should inspect this commit; do not close until that review and grouped boundary verification complete.

Implementation complete. Scoped proof: regex integration 5/5; RegexSyntax units 2/2; exact TIR Match, resident REPL, Unicode comptime/AOT parity, and focused text/regex golden pass. Both E0152 UI snapshots were generated and inspected. git diff --check is clean and tests/jit_gaps.txt did not grow. Ready for the batch's single fresh reviewer; grouped verification remains at the parent batch boundary.

Started the ratified typed Regex literal slice. I am reusing the existing typed-literal elaboration and the canonical linear regex engine; scoped tests cover inferred positional and named heads, explicit heads, compile offsets, bare strings, and runtime compile.

Owner ratified D-REGEX-LIT1 = D with a spelling correction: typed literal required, head inferable (.{"..."}), bare strings never implicit. Ballot option D amended to match; acceptance terms recorded as criteria.

criteria.text: Head inference: .{"..."} in a pattern-typed positional or named argument compile-validates and returns the match directly (no ??). Explicit Regex.{"..."} works everywhere; runtime-built patterns keep the fallible Result path.
criteria.evidence: reusable_regex_matches_across_comptime_tir_and_runtime passed exactly. Independent recheck confirmed canonical jet.regex.literal lowering and AOT replacement borrowing.

questions.text: why can't we combine b and a? Also, with inference, you wouldn't necessarily need the "Regex" prefix for literal ctor because it would be implied, but then we get consistency & any other benefits of being typed literal, all in one
questions.answer: They combine cleanly, and inference is exactly the bridge: A is B with the head inferred. A string literal in a pattern position is implicitly the Regex typed literal — compile-validated, returns the match directly, no prefix and no ??. The explicit Regex.{"..."} head is the same construct spelled out, for named reusable pattern values and anywhere inference cannot see a literal — consistent with the SQL/HTML typed-literal family. Runtime-built strings keep the fallible Result path unchanged. I added option D recording this A+B synthesis and moved the recommendation to it, so it can be ratified directly.

cards.title: E0107 says a type does not exist when it does
cards.body: Type-unification audit 2026-07-28, F5 evidence. With struct Machine and state Machine { Off, On } in scope, the expression Machine.Off fires E0107 'nothing named Machine exists here' — but Machine.make() resolves fine, so the name clearly exists. The diagnostic should say the member is missing (or that states are not values), not that the type is absent. Copy-only fix in the resolver's error path; snapshot update per I4. Note: whether states BECOME addressable is D-STATE-NS1 (separate ballot); this card only fixes the lying message.
cards.plan:
With `struct Machine` and `state Machine { Off, On }` in scope, `Machine.Off` fires E0107 "nothing named Machine exists here" while `Machine.make()` resolves fine. The message is false: the name exists.

1. In the resolver's error path, when the base name resolves but the member does not, say the member is missing, not that the type is absent.
2. Where the missing member names a state, say that states are not runtime values.
3. Copy only. Whether states become addressable is D-STATE-NS1 on card #1296; this card must not pre-empt it.
4. Update the registered text and the UI snapshot (I4).

Owned paths: the member-resolution error path in crates/jet-sema/src/Sema, the diagnostic registry, tests/ui.

Proof: a targeted test showing the new message for a state member and for an ordinary missing member; snapshots updated; independent review closes.

cards.title: Spec law: control constructs are never types; artifacts always are
cards.body: Type-unification audit 2026-07-28, F11. Add one ungated spec paragraph to the control-flow section: a control construct is an expression wherever it produces a value, and its runtime artifacts are types; the construct itself never is. Rationale in the audit (lambda duplication under I8, beginner top-to-bottom reading, zero-cost lowering, artifacts capture all the value). This paragraph is the standing answer to every future 'should loop/if/taskgroup be a type?' request.
cards.plan:
One spec paragraph, ungated by the audit. It is the standing answer to every future "should loop, if, or taskgroup be a type?" request.

1. Add the paragraph to the control-flow section of the spec: a control construct is an expression wherever it produces a value, and its runtime artifacts are types; the construct itself never is.
2. Carry the audit's argument in short form: a construct-as-value already has a name in Jet, the lambda, so a Loop or If type would be a second spelling of one mechanism (I8); the value-producing cases are already expressions; the artifacts capture all the value; and keeping constructs as keywords keeps the lowering zero-cost and keeps a beginner reading top to bottom.
3. Cross-reference the audit section so the reasoning is one click away.

Owned paths: docs/spec/spec.md (control-flow section), and a pointer from docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md if the law needs a decision row.

Proof: the paragraph reads correctly against the current control-flow surface; independent review closes.
